# CHAPTER XX

## FAILURE (1871)

Far back in childhood Henry Adams could recall his first visit to Harvard College — driven out as a boy of nine to visit his aunt in the old President's House. The house had an air of colonial self-respect that impressed even a nine-year-old child. When he closed his interview with President Eliot, Adams asked the Bursar about his aunt's old drawing-room, for the house had been turned to base uses, and took the rooms.

For the next nine months the Assistant Professor exhausted all his strength in trying to keep one day ahead of his duties. Between Gurney's classical courses and Torrey's modern ones lay a gap of a thousand years, which Adams was expected to fill. Down to the moment he took his chair and looked his scholars in the face, he had given, as far as he could remember, an hour, more or less, to the Middle Ages.

Not that his ignorance troubled him! He knew enough to be ignorant. A parent gives life, but as parent, gives no more. A murderer takes life, but his deed stops there. A teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops. A teacher must either treat history as a catalogue, a record, a romance, or as an evolution; and whether he affirms or denies evolution, he falls into all the burning faggots of the pit. He makes of his scholars either priests or atheists, plutocrats or socialists, judges or anarchists, almost in spite of himself. In essence incoherent and immoral, history had either to be taught as such — or falsified.

Adams wanted to do neither. He had no theory of evolution to teach, and could not make the facts fit one. Since Gibbon, the spectacle was almost a scandal. History had lost even the sense of shame; it was a hundred years behind the experimental sciences. The lecture system to classes of hundreds, which was very much that of the twelfth century, suited him not at all. Nine minds in ten take polish passively, like a hard surface; only the tenth sensibly reacts. Adams thought that, as no one seemed to care what he did, he would try to cultivate this tenth mind, joining his students in trying to find the best way of learning what he did not know.

The task was doomed for a reason he could not control. Nothing is easier than to teach historical method, but, when learned, it has little use. History is a tangled skein that one may take up at any point, and break when one has unravelled enough; but complexity precedes evolution. The Pteraspis grins horribly from the closed entrance. He took law as subject, the Law School as end, and half-a-dozen intelligent young men as victims of his experiment. The boys worked like rabbits, and dug holes all over the field of archaic society; but their teacher knew from his own experience that his wonderful method led nowhere.

The fault lay in the system, which could lead only to inertia. His own mind required conflict, contradiction, even more than the student's. His reform would have begun in the lecture-room at his own desk: he would have seated a rival assistant professor opposite him, whose business should be strictly limited to expressing opposite views. Nothing short of this would ever interest either the professor or the student; but of all university freaks, no irregularity shocked the intellectual atmosphere so much as contradiction or competition between teachers. In that respect the thirteenth-century university system was worth the whole teaching of the modern school.

The seven years he passed in teaching seemed to him lost. As a professor, he regarded himself as a failure. He quitted the university at last, in 1877, with a feeling that, if it had not been for the invariable courtesy and kindness shown by every one in it, he should be sore at his failure.

These were his own feelings, but they seemed not to be felt in the college. With the same perplexing impartiality that had so much disconcerted him in his undergraduate days, the college insisted on expressing an opposite view. Nothing in the vanity of life struck him as more humiliating than that Harvard College, which he had persistently criticised, abused, abandoned, and neglected, should alone have offered him a dollar, an office, an encouragement, or a kindness. Harvard College might have its faults, but at least it redeemed America, since it was true to its own.

The only part of education that the professor thought a success was the students. Cast more or less in the same mould, ignorant of all that man had ever thought or hoped, their minds burst open like flowers at the sunlight of a suggestion. Adams put the question to one of them — what could he do with his education? — and was surprised at the answer: "The degree of Harvard College is worth money to me in Chicago." This reply upset his experience; for the degree of Harvard College had been rather a drawback to a young man in Boston and Washington. His colleagues, perhaps, knew what they had to teach; he did not. He could teach his students nothing; he was only educating himself at their cost.
